title: Pre-Purchase Ship Inspection Sydney | Port Botany & Slipways
description: Pre-purchase inspection in Sydney for buyers: tankers and LPG carriers at Port Botany, cement carriers at Glebe Island, ferries and tugs on harbour slipways.
h1: Inspecting a Second-Hand Ship for a Buyer in Sydney, from the Botany Fuel Berths to the Harbour Slipways
intro: A buyer who wants to see a ship before the deal closes in Sydney usually has to fit the visit into a cargo call. Product tankers, chemical tankers and LPG carriers discharge imported fuel and gas at Port Botany, cement carriers unload at Glebe Island, and harbour ferries, tugs and workboats change hands between operators while they sit on the city's slipways. Atlantis uses that short stay for a measured pre-purchase inspection of structure, coatings, spot thickness, crack-prone details and running machinery, so the buyer decides on evidence, not impressions. The team flies from India for each inspection, and the visa and the confirmed berth window set the earliest date.

highlights.p: A laden tanker reaching the Botany fuel berths usually arrives with her ballast tanks close to empty, and the chief officer starts filling them as cargo goes ashore. Agreeing the entry order before arrival lets the buyer see the tanks that matter most while they are still dry and open to entry.

highlights.h: Domestic craft bought off the slip
highlights.p: Ferries, tugs, pilot boats and workboats are often sold while they are out of the water for maintenance. On a Sydney slipway the whole underwater hull, the propulsion openings and the shell around the fendering can be gauged and crack-checked, which is rarely possible on a vessel offered afloat.

Many buyers of ships trading to Sydney work from Singapore, Hong Kong, Athens, London or Hamburg. A summary written at the end of a Sydney working day reaches Asian desks that afternoon and European desks early in their morning, while the inspection period under the sale terms is still running.

sections.h: Where can a buyer inspect a ship in Sydney?
p: The answer depends on what the ship is doing when the seller offers the visit. At the Port Botany container terminals a ship is working cargo for about a day, the crane plan sets the pace and the holds stay full of boxes, so a buyer sees the deck, hatch coamings, lashing structure, whichever ballast tanks the chief officer can release, and the engine room. That is enough to judge the deck structure and the machinery, but not the holds.

The bulk liquids berths on the same peninsula offer a different kind of visit. A product tanker, chemical tanker or LPG carrier discharging there works under the terminal's safety regime: no hot work, controlled movement around the manifold, and cargo tanks that are anything but gas-free. The buyer's inspection therefore covers ballast spaces, deck structure, pipe supports, accommodation and machinery, and judges the cargo containment from the records and from deck.

In the inner harbour, cement and dry bulk carriers discharge at Glebe Island, where the water is sheltered and the stay can be long enough for emptied cargo spaces to be ventilated and entered under the master's permit. Few merchant ships are docked in Sydney; if a seller arranges a docking in the Captain Cook Graving Dock at Garden Island, which has to fit around the Navy's programme, the buyer gains the one chance in the city to gauge a large ship's bottom. Smaller craft are the exception to the rule: ferries, tugs, pilot boats and workboats come out of the water on harbour slipways and can be inspected all round.

Ships held off the coast waiting for a berth are a poor choice for a buyer. The waiting area lies in open water exposed to the Tasman Sea swell, launches run only in suitable weather, and an East Coast Low in late autumn or winter can stop transfers altogether while it passes. Inspecting alongside is safer and more productive, even when that means waiting for the berth.
list: Port Botany container terminals: deck, coamings, lashing bridges, releasable ballast tanks and engine room during a cargo exchange
Port Botany bulk liquids berths: ballast spaces, deck, pipe supports and machinery on tankers and LPG carriers, under the terminal's rules
Glebe Island: cargo spaces and deck of cement and dry bulk carriers once discharge has finished
Captain Cook Graving Dock, Garden Island: bottom and side shell, when a seller's docking fits the naval programme
Harbour slipways: complete hull, propulsion openings and fendering zones of ferries, tugs and workboats

sections.h: Which ships do buyers inspect in Sydney, and what are they trying to learn?
p: Sydney now imports its fuels as finished products, since both of its refineries closed, so medium-range product tankers and smaller chemical tankers are among the most frequent deep-sea callers at Botany. Buyers of those ships want to know how the ballast tanks have aged on a trade built on repeated discharge calls, whether the deck piping and its supports will soon need renewal, and whether the ship's vetting and port state history matches what they find on board. LPG carriers raise the same structural questions, with the cargo containment judged from the records the seller releases.

Cement carriers at Glebe Island are a specialised and often older type, and they tend to be sold to operators who already know the trade. Their buyers look closely at the cargo spaces, at the discharge system's pipework, where wall loss gathers at bends, and at the deck and hatch arrangements that keep the cargo dry. Container ships are bought and sold as part of deep-sea fleets and are usually inspected wherever the sale catches them, which is sometimes a Botany call.

Domestic craft form a market of their own. Harbour ferries, tugs, pilot vessels and workboats are sold between operators in New South Wales and other states, and sometimes abroad. A craft that stays in Australian domestic commercial service needs a certificate of survey under the national law for domestic commercial vessels, issued on surveys by an accredited marine surveyor or, for most vessels of 35 metres or more and for novel designs, a recognised organisation. AMSA must be told of the sale within 14 days and the buyer can take over the certificate, yet neither step shows how the hull and machinery stand today. That is the question a pre-purchase inspection answers.

sections.h: How is a pre-purchase inspection scoped around a Sydney cargo call?
p: The usable time starts later than the arrival time. A ship coming from overseas must be cleared by biosecurity before anyone from shore boards, and inside the port security zones the team is escorted from the gate to the gangway, because visitors do not carry the identification card that unescorted access requires. The plan is therefore drawn from the moment of boarding to the scheduled sailing, with the most decisive spaces placed first.

On a tanker the order is usually set by ballasting. Tank entries are requested for the first hours of the call, before water goes in, and deck work follows, keeping clear of the manifold while hoses are connected. The discharge itself helps the machinery assessment: generators and cargo pump drives are working under real load, which is when vibration and thermal readings say most. The main engine is stopped alongside and, under the usual sale terms, crankcases stay shut, so its condition is read from records and from the chief engineer's trend data.

On a slipway the order reverses. The hull is out of the water and the buyer's first concern is usually the bottom, the shell at the fendering line and the structure around propellers, rudders or waterjets, so external readings and crack checks come first and internal spaces follow. Permission to remove fendering, lift deck plates or open voids is the seller's to give, and the report records where it was withheld.

Every enclosed-space entry needs the seller's consent and the master's permit, and the team carries its own gas monitors. Grinding, opening up and coating removal are limited to what the seller agrees in writing, so most readings are taken through sound coating.

sections.h: What do pre-purchase inspections of Sydney ships typically find?
p: On fuel-trade tankers the usual findings sit in the ballast spaces and on deck: coating breakdown along stiffener edges and in the upper wing tanks, pitting in double-bottom plating, and wasted pipe supports, saddles and walkway brackets along the cargo pipe runs. Few of these items would stop a sale on their own, but together they show the buyer what the next docking will have to put right.

Cement carriers often show abrasion and condensation corrosion in their cargo spaces and thinning in the discharge pipework. Container ships show distorted coaming corners, worn lashing bridge foundations, bent cell guides and, where a scrubber is fitted, wall loss in the wash-water discharge line close to the overboard connection.

Domestic craft bring a separate set of findings. Aluminium catamaran ferries can develop fatigue cracks around engine bearers, waterjet or propeller mountings and hull-to-deck joints; aluminium is not magnetic, so those details are checked with dye penetrant, and the ultrasonic gauge is calibrated on aluminium rather than steel. Tugs carry their history at the fendering line and in the foundations of towing winches and staples, where repeated loads open cracks. Every finding is located, photographed and graded by how far it bears on the buyer's decision.

sections.h: Planning a buyer's inspection in Sydney: visas, distance and the records to request
p: Distance sets the pace. The team travels from India, Indian passport holders need an Australian visa suited to short specialist work, and processing times vary, so the application goes in as soon as the viewing is agreed in principle. The reference date is the berth window the seller's agent confirms, not the ship's first arrival off the coast; flying into Kingsford Smith, which sits beside Port Botany, keeps the last leg short once that date is firm.

Ask the seller early for what the inspection will be read against: the class status and survey records, obtained through the classification society with the seller's consent; the last thickness measurement reports; port state control results, which AMSA's inspections place in both the Tokyo MoU and Indian Ocean MoU records; and, for domestic craft, the certificate of survey with its periodic survey schedule. Send the vessel name, the berth and dates, the buyer's scope and the window in the sale terms to info@atlantisndt.com; the enquiry form lower on the page works just as well.

sections.h: Worked scope: an MR product tanker discharging at the Botany fuel berths
p: The buyer's superintendent and our planner rank the spaces before the ship arrives. The seller has agreed to entry into ballast tanks but not cargo tanks, so the first list starts with the ballast tanks that the seller's own reports flag as weakest, followed by a contrasting pair from the other end of the ship, which lets the buyer tell local damage from general condition.

Once biosecurity clearance and the terminal escort are in place, the tank entries run as discharge begins and before the chief officer ballasts those tanks. Deck plating, pipe supports and vent heads are gauged and examined away from the manifold. In the engine room, the generators and cargo pump drives are measured under discharge load and the switchboards are thermally imaged. The day ends with a call to the superintendent and a written summary of anything that could reopen the negotiation; the full report, with readings marked on the drawings, follows.

codes: Norwegian Saleform 2012 and SALEFORM 2025 – buyers' inspection and acceptance
IACS UR Z10.1 and Z10.4 – hull surveys of oil tankers and double-hull oil tankers
Marine Safety (Domestic Commercial Vessel) National Law – certificates of survey for domestic craft
ASTM E797 – manual pulse-echo ultrasonic thickness measurement
ISO 20816-1 – measurement and evaluation of machine vibration
deliverables: Same-day summary of findings that could reopen the negotiation
Ballast tank, deck and pipe-support condition, with spot readings located on the drawings
Slipway readings and crack-check results for ferries, tugs and workboats
Machinery vibration and thermal readings taken under discharge load
Notes on the class, port state control and domestic survey records the seller released
Items not inspected, with the reason each was withheld

faqs.q: Can a buyer inspect a tanker at Port Botany while she is discharging?
faqs.a: Yes, within the terminal's rules. Ballast tanks, deck structure, accommodation and machinery can all be inspected during discharge, provided the seller consents and the master issues the permits. A trading tanker's cargo tanks are never gas-free, so the buyer learns about them from the seller's records and what can be seen on deck. The most useful tank entries come early in the call, before the ship begins taking on ballast as her cargo goes ashore.

faqs.q: Can you carry out a pre-purchase inspection of a ferry or tug on a Sydney slipway?
faqs.a: Yes, and the slipway is often the best place for it. With the craft out of the water, the bottom, the shell along the fendering, the stern gear and the waterjet or propeller openings can be gauged and examined directly. Aluminium hulls are crack-checked with dye penetrant and gauged with the instrument set up for aluminium. The yard and the seller decide how long the craft stays on the slip, so the inspection is booked around their programme.

faqs.q: Does your inspection replace the AMSA survey of a domestic commercial vessel?
faqs.a: No. A domestic commercial vessel's certificate of survey depends on surveys by an accredited marine surveyor or, for most vessels of 35 metres or more and for novel designs, a recognised organisation. Our pre-purchase inspection is the buyer's own evidence of condition before the deal closes. If the buyer wishes, the readings and photographs can be passed to the surveyor handling the certificate, but they do not stand in for that survey.

faqs.q: Is it worth inspecting a ship while she waits off Sydney?
faqs.a: Rarely. Ships wait in open water outside the harbours, launches depend on swell and wind, and an East Coast Low can close the window with little warning. A wait offshore also gives no certainty about when the ship will berth. Where she will come alongside within a reasonable time, we recommend inspecting at the berth and using the waiting days to settle the scope and the permits with the seller.

faqs.q: Will the classification society accept the thickness readings from a Sydney pre-purchase inspection?
faqs.a: No, and the inspection does not need it to. For class to credit readings to a survey, the firm taking them needs IACS UR Z17 approval from that ship's own society. Atlantis has that approval in progress with DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS, and no certificate has yet been issued. Here the readings serve only the buyer's decision, read side by side with whatever class records the seller lets the society release.

faqs.q: How early should a buyer contact Atlantis about an inspection in Sydney?
faqs.a: As soon as the ship is a serious candidate, even before the viewing date is fixed. The team's Australian visa and the long journey from India set the earliest possible date, and the seller's agent needs time to arrange terminal escorts and permits. Sending the vessel name, the likely berth and the window in the sale terms to info@atlantisndt.com lets us start on the visa and the inspection plan in parallel.
